hints: Compare the positions of magnesium and calcium in Group 2 and count how many filled inner shells shield the outer electrons in each atom.
Think how the distance of the 3s electrons in Mg versus the 4s electrons in Ca from the nucleus affects the pull felt, even though Ca has more protons.
walkthrough:
Picture the two atoms side by side**
Magnesium is $\text{Mg}$ with electron arrangement 2,8,2. Calcium is $\text{Ca}$ with 2,8,8,2. So Mg uses $n=3$ for its outer electrons while Ca uses $n=4$. That extra full shell in calcium matters a lot.

Weigh nuclear charge against shielding and distance**
Yes, calcium has 20 protons compared to 12 in magnesium, so you might expect a stronger pull. But calcium also has one more inner shell. That gives more shielding and, crucially, puts the outer electrons much further from the nucleus.

Link to energy to remove electrons**
In magnesium the outer $3s$ electrons are closer in and less shielded, so the nucleus holds them more tightly. More energy is therefore needed to remove them, which is why magnesium is less reactive than calcium with cold water.

Final answer: Magnesium outer electrons experience less shielding as Mg has one fewer inner shell of electrons than Ca.
The outer electrons in Mg are closer to the nucleus, so there is stronger nuclear attraction and more energy is needed to remove them.

hints: Recall the general pattern for a Group 2 metal with cold water: metal + water gives metal hydroxide + hydrogen.
Balance the H and OH groups and then decide the correct state for Sr metal, liquid water, soluble Sr(OH)2 solution and hydrogen gas.
walkthrough:
Write the skeleton from the Group 2 pattern**
All Group 2 metals do the same thing with cold water. You get the hydroxide and hydrogen gas: $\text{Sr} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Sr(OH)}_2 + \text{H}_2$. Strontium is in oxidation state +2, so one $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ needs two $\text{OH}^{-}$.

Balance and add states**
You need $2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to supply $2\text{O}$, $2\text{H}$ for the hydroxide and $2\text{H}$ for $\text{H}_2$. The question tells you a colourless solution is seen, so $\text{Sr(OH)}_2$ is aqueous here. That gives $$\mathrm{Sr(s) + 2H_2O(l) \rightarrow Sr(OH)_2(aq) + H_2(g)}$$

hints: Both beakers make the same moles of hydroxide in principle, but a white solid remains, so think about which hydroxide dissolves more in water down Group 2.
Link the amount of dissolved hydroxide to pH by thinking about which solution releases more $\text{OH}^{-}$ ions into the $100\text{ cm}^3$ of water.
walkthrough:
Spot that solubility controls the result**
You add $0.005$ mol of each metal, so you could make $0.005$ mol of each hydroxide. But both beakers show white solid plus solution, meaning neither hydroxide has fully dissolved. Solubility, not moles added, decides pH.

Use the Group 2 solubility trend**
Hydroxide solubility increases down Group 2. $\text{Sr(OH)}_2$ is more soluble than $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$, so more of the strontium solid dissolves in the same $100\text{ cm}^3$ of water.

Connect dissolved base to alkalinity**
More dissolved $\text{Sr(OH)}_2$ means a higher concentration of $\text{OH}^{-}$ ions in solution. Higher $[\text{OH}^{-}]$ means higher pH, so the strontium beaker is more alkaline.

Final answer: Strontium produces the more alkaline solution.
Strontium hydroxide is more soluble than calcium hydroxide, so more $\text{OH}^{-}$ is in solution / it dissociates more to give a stronger base.

hints: Think what you would actually see when a solid carbonate meets excess dilute acid and what gas is released.
walkthrough:
Visualise carbonate in acid**
Magnesium carbonate is a white solid. With excess dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ it reacts to form soluble $\text{MgSO}_4$ plus $\text{CO}_2$ gas: $$\text{MgCO}_3\text{(s)} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{MgSO}_4\text{(aq)} + \text{CO}_2\text{(g)} + \text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$$ You see fizzing as $\text{CO}_2$ bubbles off and the white solid disappears.
Final answer: Effervescence / bubbles of gas seen and white solid dissolves to give a colourless solution.

hints: Use the +2 oxidation state of X in the oxide to work out the charge on the ion and the formula pattern compared with $\text{MO}$ for Group 2.
Look at what happens to $\text{XCO}_3$ on heating and compare it with the known behaviour of Group 2 carbonates.
Compare the colours described, black oxide and green carbonate, with the typical colours of Group 2 oxides and carbonates.
walkthrough:
Pull out the +2 clue**
You are told X is +2 in the oxide. Group 2 metals also always form $\text{M}^{2+}$. That is similarity one, and it explains why the carbonate is $\text{XCO}_3$, exactly like $\text{CaCO}_3$ or $\text{MgCO}_3$.

Match the reaction types**
$\text{XCO}_3$ decomposes on heating to oxide plus a colourless gas. That is exactly what Group 2 carbonates do: carbonate to oxide + $\text{CO}_2$. Also the oxide must be $\text{XO}$, the same 1:1 stoichiometry as $\text{MgO}$, $\text{CaO}$ etc. Any two such similarities earn the two marks.

Spot the colour contrast**
Group 2 compounds are almost always white. Here the oxide is black and the carbonate is green. That colour is the clear difference, and it hints X is actually a transition metal such as copper or nickel, not Group 2.

Final answer: Similarity 1: X forms a +2 ion / has +2 oxidation state, same as Group 2.
Similarity 2: forms an oxide XO with same stoichiometry as Group 2 oxides MO / carbonate decomposes on heating to oxide + carbon dioxide, same as Group 2.
Difference 1: X forms coloured oxide / carbonate (black oxide, green carbonate) whereas Group 2 oxides and carbonates are white.

hints: Combine the +2 charge on X with the 2- charge on oxide to work out the simplest neutral formula.
walkthrough:
Balance the charges**
X is $\text{X}^{2+}$ and oxide is $\text{O}^{2-}$. One of each balances to neutral, so the formula is simply $\text{XO}$.

hints: Remember carbonate decomposition always splits the carbonate into the matching oxide plus carbon dioxide.
walkthrough:
Write the decomposition pattern**
Heating a carbonate drives off $\text{CO}_2$ and leaves the oxide behind. Using your formula $\text{XO}$ from the last part: $$\text{XCO}_3\text{(s)} \rightarrow \text{XO(s)} + \text{CO}_2\text{(g)}$$ The equation is already balanced with 1:1:1 stoichiometry.
